intro: CLI, harness, session, context, slash commands: the words people use about Claude Code, explained.

1.summary: Model vs harness, CLI, session and context window.

lesson.title: Claude Code = a model + a harness
lesson.body:
The **model** is the brain: Claude Opus, Sonnet or Haiku. On its own, a model can only read text and write text back.

The **harness** is everything wrapped around the brain so it can do real work. It gives the model **tools** (read files, run commands, search), **rules** (what needs your permission), and **memory** of the conversation so far.

Picture a brilliant consultant (the model) vs. that consultant plus an office, a keycard, a phone and a rulebook (the harness). **Claude Code is a harness.** So are Cursor, Cline and Copilot's agent mode, often running the same models.
lesson.pm: When comparing AI coding tools, ask two separate questions: which *model* does it use, and how good is its *harness*? Two tools with the same model can perform very differently.

lesson.title: CLI, sessions and the context window
lesson.body:
A **CLI** (command-line interface) is an app you use by typing instead of clicking. Claude Code started as a CLI: you open the terminal and type `claude`. It now also runs in a desktop app, in VS Code and on the web, but it's the same harness underneath.

A **session** is one continuous conversation with Claude Code, with everything it has read and done along the way.

The **context window** is the model's working memory: the maximum amount of text it can "see" at once. Your messages, every file it reads and every command output all go into it.
lesson.pm: Long, sprawling sessions fill the context window with old material. Starting a fresh session for a new task often gets better results.

cards.back: The AI brain (e.g. Claude Opus). It reads text and writes text. It can't act on its own.
The program around a model that gives it tools, rules and memory so it can do real work. Claude Code is a harness.
Command-line interface: an app you use by typing commands in a terminal instead of clicking.
One continuous conversation with Claude Code, including everything it read and did.
The model's working memory: the maximum amount of text it can consider at once.
An action the harness lets the model take, like reading a file or running a command.

quiz.q: Cursor and Claude Code can both use Claude Sonnet. So what's actually different between them?
options: The harness: tools, rules, prompts and workflow around the model
quiz.why: Same brain, different harness. The harness decides which tools exist, how context is managed and how you interact.
A command-line interface is an app you operate by typing text commands.

quiz.q: Claude Code reads 40 large files in one session. What fills up?
quiz.why: Everything read or produced in a session lands in the context window, the model's working memory.

quiz.q: On its own, without a harness, what can a model do?
options: Take in text and produce text
quiz.why: Models just produce text. Actions happen when the harness turns that text into real tool calls.

quiz.q: You're switching from fixing a bug to writing docs about something unrelated. Good practice?
options: Start a fresh session so old context doesn't distract the model
Keep going in the same session forever
quiz.why: A clean context window keeps the model focused on what matters now.

2.summary: Commands vs prompts, tokens, compaction and CLAUDE.md.

lesson.title: "Command" means three different things
lesson.body:
People say "command" for three different things:

1. A **terminal command**, like `ls` or `git status`, is run by the shell (the terminal's command reader), not by AI.
2. A **slash command**, like `/clear`, `/model` or `/help`, is a shortcut you type in Claude Code to trigger an action instead of chatting. Teams can also make custom ones.
3. A **prompt** is a plain-English request to the model: "fix the login bug."

When Claude Code runs a terminal command for you, you'll see it as a **Bash** tool call.
lesson.pm: Custom slash commands are a great way for a team to package a repeatable workflow ("/release-notes") so everyone does it the same way.

lesson.title: Tokens, compaction and CLAUDE.md
lesson.body:
Models read and write in **tokens**: chunks of text roughly ¾ of a word each. Context size and pricing are both measured in tokens.

When a session's context window gets full, Claude Code **compacts**: it summarizes older parts of the conversation to make room. That's why details from much earlier can get fuzzy. You can also type `/compact` yourself, or `/clear` to start fresh.

**CLAUDE.md** is a plain text file in your project that Claude Code reads at the start of every session: standing instructions like "we use Bitbucket, run tests with npm test." It's the project's briefing document.
lesson.pm: A good CLAUDE.md is like good onboarding docs for a new hire. It's one of the highest-leverage things a team can write.

cards.back: A shortcut typed in Claude Code (e.g. `/clear`, `/model`) that triggers an action instead of sending a chat message.
A plain-language request or instruction you give the model.
A chunk of text (about ¾ of a word) that models read and write in. Context and cost are measured in tokens.
Claude Code summarizing older conversation to free up room in a full context window.
A file of standing project instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of every session.
Claude Code pausing to ask you before doing something that changes things, like editing a file or running a command.

quiz.q: You type `/clear` in Claude Code. What happens?
options: The conversation's context is cleared so you start fresh
It runs a terminal command called clear on your server
It sends a message to Claude asking what clear means
quiz.why: Slash commands trigger built-in actions. `/clear` resets the conversation context.

quiz.q: Which of these is a *terminal* command rather than a slash command or a prompt?
quiz.why: `git status` is run by the shell. The slash ones are Claude Code shortcuts; the sentence is a prompt.

quiz.q: Late in a long session, Claude seems to have forgotten a detail from the start. The likely reason?
options: Older context was compacted (summarized) to make room
quiz.why: When context fills up, older parts are summarized, and summaries lose detail.

quiz.q: Where should "always run tests with `npm test` before committing" live so every session knows it?
options: In your first message each time
quiz.why: CLAUDE.md is loaded automatically at the start of every session. That's what it's for.

quiz.q: Roughly how many tokens is a 750-word document?
quiz.why: A token is about ¾ of a word, so 750 words ≈ 1,000 tokens.
